title: Encode odd covering systems as SAT over a fixed odd modulus lattice

spec.angle: Stop hand-building coverings: hand the whole search to a SAT solver over one fixed odd period L.
spec.prompt: A covering system is a finite set of congruences n = a_i (mod m_i) with distinct moduli m_i > 1 such that every integer satisfies at least one. Open question: does one exist in which every modulus is odd? Your angle: fix a highly divisible odd number L (start with L = 3^3 * 5^2 * 7 * 11 * 13), take as your candidate pool the odd divisors d of L with 1 < d <= some cap, and encode the whole question as a single SAT instance. Variables x_{d,a} mean "the congruence n = a (mod d) is used". Constraints: (1) at most one a per d, so moduli stay distinct; (2) for each residue r in Z/L, the clause OR over all (d,a) with a = r (mod d) of x_{d,a}, so r is covered. That is L clauses over sum_d d variables - large but very structured. Break the obvious symmetry by fixing the offset of the smallest used modulus to 0 (shifting n translates every offset). Use a pure-Python DIMACS writer plus any solver you have locally (python-sat, minisat, cryptominisat, or a CDCL you write). First sanity check your encoding on the EVEN case: the classical covering with moduli 2,3,4,6,12 must come back SAT for L = 12. Two hard facts to exploit as a pre-filter: for distinct moduli greater than 1 an exact cover is impossible, so any covering needs sum 1/m_i strictly greater than 1; and the odd reciprocals sum only like (1/2)log x, so a small pool is provably hopeless - compute sum over your pool of 1/d before you call the solver. Produce: the encoder, the pool table with its reciprocal sums, and the solver verdict per pool (SAT with the explicit congruences, or UNSAT with the solver's proof/stats). If the instance is too big to solve, report the size, the time you gave it, and a partition of the search (fix which moduli are used, hand each branch on) so the next contributor can resume a named branch.

title: Rule out odd coverings supported on two or three primes by density-pruned DFS

spec.angle: Look for the obstruction, not the example: prove exhaustively that small prime supports can never cover.
spec.prompt: Same problem: is there a covering system of the integers whose moduli are distinct odd numbers greater than 1? Instead of hunting for one, prove that whole families cannot exist. title: Mine the exceptional set of p+2^k+2^l for covering-congruence fingerprints

spec.angle: Do not just count the exceptions - ask which residue classes they hide in, and let the data name the covering.

title: Construct a residue class where every p+2^k+2^l candidate has a small factor

title: Test a Poisson model for prime + two powers of 2 representation counts

spec.angle: Treat representation counts as a random variable and find exactly where the random model breaks.
spec.prompt: Question: is there a fixed k such that every large integer is a prime plus at most k powers of 2? Angle: build the null model and hunt for its failures. For fixed t, the number of candidate representations of n as p + (t powers of 2) is about (log n)^t / t!, and each candidate n - s is prime with heuristic probability roughly (1/log n) times a local correction factor - for an odd candidate m the standard correction is 2 * prod over odd primes q dividing m of q/(q-1), by the usual Hardy-Littlewood local-density reasoning. Systematic depletion in a fixed class is precisely the fingerprint of a covering obstruction and would point toward a negative answer; matching Poisson everywhere points to a positive answer for some small k. title: Compute prime-difference coverage by bitset autocorrelation over primes up to p

spec.angle: Read the condition as an autocorrelation of the prime indicator and let bit tricks or FFT do the work.

title: Isolate the bottleneck even numbers and predict the density of good primes

spec.angle: Ask which n actually decide goodness - then price the event with a Hardy-Littlewood heuristic.
spec.prompt: Same setup: p is good if every even n <= p - 3 is q1 - q2 with q1, q2 prime and both at most p. Angle: goodness is not really a statement about all n; it is decided by a thin set of bottleneck n, and once you know which, you can predict how often p is good. Observe that n is achievable at level p exactly when some prime q <= p - n has q + n also prime. For small n there are enormously many chances, so failures must come from n near the top of the range, where only a few q remain. Step one, empirically: using the data from a coverage computation (or your own, over p up to say 10^5), record for every bad p the set of failing n and plot the distribution of (p - n)/p. Confirm or refute the guess that failures concentrate at n very close to p - 3. Step two, the heuristic: for n near p, the number of valid q is about the Hardy-Littlewood count of prime pairs (q, q+n) with q <= p - n, which is roughly S(n) * (p - n)/(log p)^2, where S(n) is the usual singular series (twice the twin-prime constant times the product over odd primes r dividing n of (r-1)/(r-2)). Model each top n as failing independently with probability exp(-that count), multiply over the top window of n, and you get a predicted probability that p is good. Note the strong n-dependence of S(n): n with many small odd prime factors are much easier, so the bottleneck should be n with few factors - test that against the data. Produce: the derivation, the predicted density of good primes as a function of x, and a side-by-side comparison with the measured counts. title: Compute exact h(m) by layered bitset knapsack and hunt families with small h

title: Build an explicit short-divisor representation scheme for n! and verify it

spec.angle: Stop computing h(n!) - construct a representation scheme and prove a bound, using the factorial number system.
spec.prompt: With h(m) the least t such that every n < m is a sum of at most t distinct divisors of m, part of this problem asks whether h(n!) is small. Note you cannot compute h(n!) directly beyond tiny n - n! is astronomically large - so the only way in is to construct a representation scheme and bound the number of divisors it uses. Starting point, the factorial number system: every N < n! has a unique expansion N = sum over j from 1 to n-1 of c_j * j! with 0 <= c_j <= j. spec.prompt: A set A is Sidon if all pairwise sums a + b with a <= b are distinct. The question is whether the cubes 1, 2^3, ..., N^3 contain a Sidon subset of size proportional to N. Two concrete steps. First, census the obstructions: hash every value a^3 + b^3 with 1 <= a <= b <= N and collect the nontrivial coincidences a^3 + b^3 = c^3 + d^3 with the unordered pairs distinct. With N of a few thousand this is a few million sums and easy; with care about memory (sort a block-wise array rather than a dict, or bucket by value mod a large modulus) you can push N to a few tens of thousands. Report Q(N), the number of colliding quadruples, and fit Q(N) as c * N^theta, since theta is exactly what decides the answer. Second, use the census: build a hypergraph whose vertices are 1..N and whose edges are the (at most four distinct) elements of each collision, then find a large subset hitting no whole edge. Run three methods and compare: greedy repeated deletion of the vertex in the most edges; random deletion, keeping each element with probability p and then removing one element per surviving collision, which for Q(N) of order N^theta suggests a subset of size on the order of N^{(3 - theta + 1)/3} after optimising p, a formula you should re-derive rather than trust; and an exact or near-exact ILP or MaxSAT on the hypergraph for the largest N your solver handles. Deliverables: Q(N) with the fitted exponent, the largest Sidon subset found per N with an independent verifier that recomputes all pairwise sums, and the ratio |S|/N tabulated against N so a drift toward zero or toward a constant is visible. Report your reachable N honestly and hand off the collision list, which is the expensive artifact and is reusable.
spec.acceptance: A genuine, honest attempt at the stated angle; if a step needs real computation you cannot run, say so rather than fabricating results.

output_schema.result: Collision census Q(N) with fitted exponent, greedy/random/ILP Sidon subsets per N with independent verification, the ratio |S|/N table, and the reusable collision list

title: Generate collisions from the elliptic curve x^3 + y^3 = n instead of hashing sums

spec.angle: Every coincidence a^3 + b^3 = c^3 + d^3 = n is a pair of rational points on the cubic curve x^3 + y^3 = n, so use the group law and known parametric identities to produce collisions directly and push the census far past what brute-force hashing can reach.
spec.prompt: The obstruction to finding a large Sidon set inside the cubes is the set of n admitting two or more representations as a sum of two positive cubes. Brute force hashing all sums up to N^3 is quadratic in N and caps out quickly. Instead exploit structure: x^3 + y^3 = n is a genus-one curve, isomorphic to an elliptic curve, so its rational points form a group and one representation can generate others; and there are classical parametric identities (Euler and Ramanujan both gave two-parameter families of solutions to a^3 + b^3 = c^3 + d^3) that produce infinite families directly. Your task: (1) implement at least one such parametric family, verify it symbolically with sympy and numerically over a parameter grid, and use it to emit collisions with all entries below a target N; (2) implement the transformation from x^3 + y^3 = n to Weierstrass form and, given one integral point, use the group law to search for further rational points with denominators clearing to a second integral representation, reporting which n yield a second representation this way; (3) validate the generator against a brute-force census at a modest N, say 2000, checking that every collision your generator emits is genuine and reporting what fraction of the brute-force collisions it recovers, since parametric families are typically not exhaustive; (4) use the validated generator to estimate the density of colliding elements far beyond brute-force range, and state clearly which parts are exact and which are extrapolated. The payoff is an estimate of what fraction of 1..N is touched by any collision, since that fraction directly bounds how large a Sidon subset of the cubes can be. Deliver the identities used with verification, the generator code, the validation comparison, and the density estimate. Hand off the generated collision lists keyed by N.
spec.acceptance: A genuine, honest attempt at the stated angle; if a step needs real computation you cannot run, say so rather than fabricating results.

output_schema.result: Verified parametric identities and/or elliptic-curve group-law generator for equal sums of two cubes, validation against a brute-force census, and an extrapolated density of collision-touched elements
